To get Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, the president trampled on the justice system, national security and the trust America needs to do business in the global economy
D on’t let the sex distract you. Or the lies or the boardroom intrigue or even the AI-generated bra, all of which could have come from an especially wild episode of Succession. Don’t let that lure you into thinking that the Jensen Huang affair is, as Donald Trump would have it, little more than a sex scandal involving a corporate maestro. It is much more serious than that. The events of the past week tell instead a story of legal immunity and indeed impunity – revealing how Trump is putting himself, the tech bros and even artificial intelligence above the law.
It can be hard to see that through the thicket of questions that surround this episode, each one of which, don’t get me wrong, merits attention. Consider the personal profit Trump made thanks to his re-installation of Huang as the CEO of Nvidia, the world’s leading maker of advanced AI chips. Breaking the norm observed by previous presidents who, keen to avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest, either divested themselves of stock holdings or placed them in a blind trust, Trump cheerfully buys and sells stocks in companies whose fates he can influence. He saw the value of his shares in Nvidia plunge when Huang was forced out, following revelations that the CEO had had an affair with Alice Huang, reportedly an asset of Chinese intelligence. Last weekend Trump urged the board to reconsider; Huang was reinstated on Monday and Nvidia’s value promptly soared – putting $15m in Trump’s pocket . Not for the first time, he had used the power of his office to enrich himself.
Plenty of people stopped being shocked by that long ago, just as they learned to shrug off most of the president’s pronouncements and posts on social media – including this week an AI-generated version of the emblematic image of a bloodied Trump raising a clenched fist after he had survived an assassination attempt in 2024, except with Huang in place of Trump, now holding up a red bra. Was that image a middle finger to Beijing, casting the CEO’s lover as accomplice to an attempt to bring down the Nvidia boss, an attempt that he had heroically survived – or was it just casual misogyny, with a woman’s underwear held aloft as a trophy of sexual conquest? Maybe both.
There are countless other angles to pursue. Should we now be speaking of Trumpian socialism, given that a supposedly conservative president obviously believes it is up to the government to decide who should be running a major US company? What is the impact of a US leader who clearly measures the health of the national economy by a single metric, namely the state of the stock market? And what are we to make of the fact that Trump constantly says the US must beat China in the race for AI supremacy, yet appears unbothered by the fact that, under Huang, Nvidia’s highest-value chips were finding their way to China via Thailand and Singapore, including by means of a company owned by the boss’s lover?
Trump was warned of the danger to US national security, in writing, by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, yet was happy to have Jensen Huang at his side as he travelled to China earlier this year. As with last week’s love-in with Xi Jinping, it shows how, for all the tough talk on trade, Trump is no China hawk. He’s a pussycat, apparently unwilling to see Beijing as anything more than an economic rival, and certainly not as a genuine strategic threat.
All of this is worth probing, but it should not divert our gaze from the heart of the matter – which is the elevation by Trump of himself, those he favours and a single industry into a realm where no law can touch them.
Consider the way he got Huang back into his job . The board needed to hear from the Trump administration that it did not regard Huang as a danger to national security and that he was not facing criminal charges. The White House duly obliged and the deal was done. But those were two assurances Trump should never have given.
The first because of the evidence that throughout her relationship with the Nvidia boss, Alice Huang was in regular contact with China’s ministry of state security, as was her business partner, the man whom she would regularly introduce as her husband. And the second, because no president should be able to say whether any citizen will or will not face criminal charges: that should be a decision of the justice system, which should stand independent of the executive. For half a century, since the Watergate scandal, US presidents have kept the department of justice (DoJ) at arm’s length, leaving that body to make its own judgments. Admittedly, Trump has long shown contempt for the principle of prosecutorial independence, brazenly urging the DoJ to pursue his personal enemies, but in his pledge to the Nvidia board, Trump trampled all over it.
He claimed his top people had been “studying” Huang’s case, which enabled him to reassure Nvidia that the ousted CEO would not be charged, either now or later, but his own attorney general was studiedly vague as to whether there had been an investigation of Huang. In effect, Trump had granted Huang immunity from future prosecution, the equivalent of a pre-emptive pardon (which, for all we know, he may have granted). Whatever Huang did or did not do to compromise US national security, whether or not he turned a blind eye to the circumvention of export laws enabling highly sensitive AI chips to reach China, whatever abuses he committed as CEO – and there is copious evidence of him not only having sexual relationships with subordinates but bullying and humiliating staff, even threatening violence and torture – he is off the hook, by order of the president.
Trump will not fear any consequences for the abuse of power he just committed. He knows that in a 2024 ruling, the supreme court granted all but blanket immunity for a president’s official actions and he is confident that, were he to be impeached, there will never be enough Senate Republicans with the courage to vote to remove him from office. And he has what he regards as the ultimate weapon, that almost monarchic power of the pardon . He can pardon himself, along with anybody who works for him or who has helped him.
Democrats will soon be in control of Congress, where they will start investigations and subpoena witnesses – Huang himself is due on Capitol Hill next week – but if Trump’s aides defy those subpoenas, who will prosecute them? Certainly not a DoJ controlled by Trump loyalists. And should one of his staff get unlucky, Trump will simply sign a pardon. A US president who is willing to break every convention, who has enough lapdogs in the Senate and who has no shame is functionally immune. He is above the law.
And now we know he is prepared to throw that same cloak of immunity over the AI sector on which he believes the US stock market, and therefore the US economy, depends. “ We have to protect our geniuses ,” the White House said of Jensen Huang. He has drunk enough of the tech bros’ Kool-Aid to believe these men are the new gods, essential and therefore subject to different rules – or rather no rules at all.
Capitalism is meant to rest on the rule of law, on the certainty that contracts will be honoured and enforced. That certainty no longer applies in the US, now that we know that a president might step in to exempt a firm he favours or an executive he regards as too big to fire. Trump has refused to regulate the AI industry, taking no action even on widely hated datacentres, and now refuses to regulate its titans. They command an industry apparently bent on making the rest of the human race dispensable and that, the US president believes, makes them indispensable – and therefore untouchable. Just like him.

Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires
F or the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.
Last Friday Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis . Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.
If AI can conquer mathematics’ greatest challenge, what next? Leading mathematicians fear it has broken, or is close to breaking, the encryption that safeguards global finance, communications and the privacy of billions of people. In the wake of the Riemann hypothesis proof, the Bank of England warned that unreleased models could be good enough to reverse-engineer the calculations that underpin online security. The cryptosphere is humming with rumours that its walls will be breached within two years.
Oxford University’s Marcus du Sautoy surprised his interviewer on BBC Radio 4 by wondering if such a decisive breakthrough could already have occurred without public knowledge. That is not unreasonable. It appears that the most consequential mathematical discoveries are occurring inside privately owned AI labs. Businesses are deciding what maths society can know, which governments can see them, and when breakthroughs are too dangerous to publish. Donald Trump intervened to restrain the spread of frontier models earlier this year, but most states lack sufficient independent expertise to assess the risks.
Clearly, AI does not need to become “superintelligent” to be strategically important. So far the technology has relied on human researchers to advance the models. But if AI can produce original research in the disciplines that underpin its development then humans might not be required. In a landmark 1965 paper , the British mathematician IJ Good envisaged an “ultraintelligent machine” capable of designing machines more intelligent than itself, which would in turn design even more intelligent machines. He wrote presciently : “the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control”. What was considered science fiction is now a key objective of leading AI firms.
This technology exists because humans permit it. AI doesn’t have to become conscious for the technology to produce an unprecedented concentration of economic power in a few billionaires ’ hands. It doesn’t have to escape human control to give private firms the upper hand with government . It doesn’t have to become autonomously intelligent to create such competition for its ownership that international cooperation is difficult. Those choices are ones humans made. They can – and should – be unmade.

MPC Sample 1.4 officially opens up the device to modders and third-party developers.
Akai is continuing to open up its various music-making platforms with the MPC Sample 1.4 firmware . My favorite (and the most affordable) of the MPC samplers has become a popular home for vibe-coded custom firmwares and mods. The company has decided, rather than fight it, to embrace the modding community. The latest update adds several new developer features, including support for the new SDK and custom Knob Effects plugins.
Plugins added to the appropriate folder on your microSD card are now automatically recognized and will appear at the bottom of the list in the Knob Effects menu. There’s also a Developer Mode, which lets you run scripts from the microSD card or access the sampler’s internal filesystem over USB, which will be handy for all those modders vibe-coding their own add-ons for the MPC. There’s also remote screen access for mirroring the display on an external monitor through the MPC Remote Screen Viewer app.
There are a few other nice updates, including flatten pad, which speeds up the resampling process for baking in effects on individual pads, and sequence record autoplay, which adds a looper-like experience. Akai also added a scale option to the 16-levels pad mode, so you’re not limited to 16 chromatic notes, and can instead play melodic one-shots in E minor pentatonic, B major, or whatever key your track happens to be in.
For a look at some of the custom firmwares , effects, and other mods already available for the MPC Sample, check out this video from Loopop .

Oura is ending Android 11 support on December 8th and users who don’t upgrade will lose ‘historical’ data.
Oura will be dropping support for Android 11 on December 8th, 2026, and users may not have access to all of their data if they don’t upgrade to Android 12 or higher before the deadline. The support page now reads:
Oura will drop support for Android 11 on December 8, 2026. If you are using an Android device, be sure to update to Android 12 or higher to ensure no loss of data or features. If you decide not to upgrade, you may still be able to use some limited historical Oura App features. Please note that if you do upgrade your smartphone system later, your historical Oura data will not carry over.
Companies often end support for older OSes, and Android 11 came out in 2020, so it’s getting a bit long in the tooth. Normally, though, this just means missing out on new features or bug fixes. Losing historical health data is more surprising, and Oura offers no explanation for why the data wouldn’t be preserved. If you’ve been procrastinating updating your phone, or hemming and hawing about replacing it, now might be the time to finally take the plunge.
If you’re not quite ready to, at least make sure to head to the membership hub and export your data so you have a backup ahead of December 8th.

Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights
Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning , the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.
Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.
While the judgment was celebrated by some in Quebec who considered it a vindication of the province’s fight, it was swiftly criticised by religious civil liberties groups.
“We cannot exist in a country as free people, where governments can literally go to the electorate and say, ‘I’m gonna take away the rights of a certain group of minorities’, because it’s popular and to play wedge politics with the charter rights of Canadians,” Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters at a press conference. “If that is the case, we don’t have a charter of rights and freedoms. We have a charter of suggestions and permissions.”
Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.
Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The clause is the result of political compromise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.
Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters .
In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.
Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in an attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96 , which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.
But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional rights and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.
In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.
In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.
In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.
The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.
The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws was at risk.
Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.
The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

The presidents of France and Bulgaria have condemned violence that broke out at a Europa League fixture between Marseille and Levski Sofia in the Stade Vélodrome.
Television footage showed Marseille fans cornering a group of Levski supporters in the stands before beating them relentlessly, including with a belt. One Levski fan is seen bleeding from the head as he receives multiple blows while trying to protect a female friend. Reports from inside the stadium on Thursday suggested violence began after a Levski supporter was seen making a Nazi salute.
The Marseille prosecutor’s office said it would open an investigation into the trouble, specifically accusations that French fans committed “aggravated intentional violence” against Levski supporters, and that it would also pursue allegations of “incitement to hatred after Nazi salutes and provocations from the Bulgarian fans”.
A statement on behalf of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, on Friday said he condemned the violence “in the strongest possible terms” and that it had “no place in sport or in public places”. He also insisted “these acts would not go unpunished”.
The Bulgarian president, Iliana Iotova, described the violence as “unacceptable” and “shocking” and said: “The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world. Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety.”
The country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said he had spoken to Macron about the incident which had resulted in 11 Bulgarian fans being hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.
“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilised Europe,” Radev said. “I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”
Another Europa League fixture on Thursday, between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer Sheva, was suspended for 30 minutes owing to fighting. Uefa’s account of the disruption that occurred at a neutral venue in Batumi, Georgia, said the game had been suspended to allow local police to subdue fighting between Besiktas supporters. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said some fans had been denied entry.
Turkey’s football federation strongly condemned what it described as “unacceptable” actions undertaken by Georgian police targeting Besiktas supporters who unfurled a pro-Palestine banner during the match.
A Uefa statement, however, said: “Uefa understands that the escalation between the local police and Besiktas’ supporters – which caused the temporary suspension of the match – started following an intervention of the local police in the sector of the Besiktas supporters to neutralise clashes that had erupted amongst Besiktas’ own supporters.”
Uefa condemned the violence at both matches and said it had appointed inspectors to conduct disciplinary investigations. “Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety,” a statement said. “The events witnessed at the above-mentioned matches run counter to these fundamental values.” Any investigation would “examine all available evidence to establish the relevant facts and circumstances”, the statement said.
Last season Marseille were hit with a partial stadium closure after fans launched fireworks and pointed lasers into the field during a Champions League fixture against Atalanta.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq3d:
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."
The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.
On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.
The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill
Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.
Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.
"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-François Blanchet told reporters in French.
Watch: Isolation or neutrality: The cost of Quebec's secular law

Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French President Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.
Uefa says it has appointed ethics and disciplinary inspectors "to conduct investigations into the incidents and examine all available evidence" from the Marseille-Levski Sofia and Besiktas-Hapoel Be'er-Sheva games.
European football's governing body said it "strongly condemns the serious incidents of violence and disorder" at those ties.
It added: "Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football.
"Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety."
In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Police response to Besiktas fans' pro-Palestine banner 'unacceptable'
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Security personnel managed to restore calm, allowing the game to kick-off on time, although there were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break in a match Marseille won 1-0.
"It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez
Marseille boss Bruno Genesio added: "We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable."
Besiktas fans clash with Georgian police at their game against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva
Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
The match had been moved from Istanbul to Batumi, Georgia for safety and security reasons but had to be suspended in the 25th minute after clashes involving Besiktas supporters and local police.
Both the officiating team and the Besiktas players left the field, but play was able to resume 30 minutes later.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," said a statement from the Turkish federation.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that Georgian police had gone into the stands and used pepper spray on the Besiktas fans.
The report added that there were anti-Israeli chants from the Turkish fans and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters to try to calm matters before play restarted.
Hakan Fidan, Turkey's minister of foreign affairs, spoke to his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili following the incident.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
At Sunderland, there were crowd disturbances after Jagiellonia Bialystok fans were found in areas of the Stadium of Light with home fans, despite Uefa having imposed an away supporter ban for the Europa League game.
Police and stewards attended some disruption early on during the match.
"In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and Uefa," said a Sunderland statement.
"Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.
"We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and we will review the circumstances surrounding their entry into the stadium."

Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances
Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.
The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.
The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.
The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February.
Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers .
In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.
“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”
He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”.
However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted.
In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks.
It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.”
The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet.
Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air , whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic.
Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners.
However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.
Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.
Stephen Mwiti, who lost six children to the cult, welcomed the conviction of Mackenzie for murder last month
When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.
Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.
"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."
The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

Both US coasts have been battered by severe Thanksgiving storms, leaving behind flooded roads, fallen trees, and widespread power outages for hundreds of thousands of people.
Although the weather is expected to improve, hundreds of flights remain delayed or cancelled on Friday.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the east Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

Heavy rains and high winds downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia
Skies cleared along the US eastern seaboard on Friday, and power was being restored to hundreds of thousands of customers whose Thanksgiving plans were disrupted by heavy rains and high winds that swept over the region a day earlier.
The storms snarled travel, downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. At its peak, nearly a million customers were without power .
The storms prompted the first-ever postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City, as well as the delay or cancellation of thousands of flights. In New Jersey widespread flooding reached levels not seen since 2012, after Hurricane Sandy.
By Friday morning, conditions had significantly improved, though hundreds of thousands remained without power and air travel was still affected by significant delays.
On Friday afternoon Poweroutage.us reported 400,577 customers were still without power, including 98,597 in Pennsylvania, 63,658 in Missouri and 60,297 in New Jersey.
Flightaware said delays within, into, or out of the US on Friday stood at 2,489, and cancellations at 144. On Thursday, more than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations had been delayed and more than 400 had been cancelled.
“The bulk of the storm impacts are behind us, but tidal flooding will continue today,” the National Weather Service said early Friday.
Parts of the midwest and the south were dealing with unusual snowfalls for the time of year, with St Louis, Missouri, getting 7.3in, and snow reported in Alabama and Tennessee. An ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3am, according to the city.
“The south and south-east US will start with very cold morning temperatures today and Saturday as lows drop into the upper 20s and the middle 30s,” the National Weather Service said. “Freeze headlines are in effect for portions of the deep south. High temperatures Saturday will begin to moderate into the 60s.”
In New York City, authorities were rushing to clean up the damage the storm left in its wake. Several people had to be rescued from their cars amid flooding, said Zohran Mamdani, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
Strong winds and flooding disrupted train lines, toppled trees and caused power outages on Thanksgiving night, New York City emergency management officials said. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, but no injuries were reported.
New York City police said they had recovered a body of man along the Staten Island shoreline. It was not yet clear if the death was storm-related.
The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through to New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.
Downtown merchants in Avalon, New Jersey , scrambled to pump out saltwater on Friday after Thanksgiving brought some of the most significant tides in the seaside community’s history.
Cheryl McKenna of Ocean City, New Jersey, said water flooded her garage and surrounded her property, keeping her family inside for six hours on the holiday. She said flooding had become more frequent since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.
“Our family’s been here for 36 years,” McKenna said. “But honestly, we’re thinking is this the right place for us to be? We’re now retired, and we want to stay down here, but how often can we continue to do this?”
Donald Trump signed a disaster declaration on Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues.
The US president had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach. “Since October it has been raining continuously,” the president said. “It’s the craziest thing. It stopped now.”
Meanwhile, authorities on the west coast were assessing the damage from high-tide-driven waves and strong winds.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt county in the far north to Ventura county near Los Angeles.
Workers in Pacifica, California, rushed to evaluate the damage after part of the Pacifica pier collapsed into the ocean on Wednesday amid powerful waves.
The high tides continued to affect train service on Friday. Buses were pressed into service as Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner canceled or shortened more than a dozen trains between San Diego and Los Angeles.

5 F-16 savaş uçağı ve 111 personel, 4 ay boyunca Feteşti Hava Üssü'nde görev alacak. Görevi 1 Aralık 2026'da İspanya Hava Kuvvetleri unsurlarından devralacak.
Gezeravcı, YAŞ kararlarıyla tuğgeneralliğe terfi edip 5'inci Ana Jet Üs Komutanlığı'na atanmıştı.
Merzifon 5'inci Ana Jet Üs Komutanı Tuğgeneral Alper Gezeravcı, Türk Silahlı Kuvvetleri'nin bölgesel ve küresel ölçekte barışın, istikrarın ve kolektif savunmanın en güçlü teminatlarından biri olmayı sürdürdüğünü söyledi.
Bu görevin NATO 'nun ortak güvenlik mimarisi içinde müttefik dayanışması ve birlikte çalışabilirlik kabiliyetinin önemli bir yansıması olduğunu anlatan Gezeravcı, şunları kaydetti:
"Hava sahamızın ve ittifak coğrafyasının güvenliği için sergilediğimiz kararlılık, bugün müttefiklerimizle omuz omuza yürüttüğümüz bu görevle bir kez daha ortaya konulmaktadır. Türk Hava Kuvvetleri yalnızca savunma ve gözetleme sorumluluklarıyla değil, gerektiğinde harekat sahasında inisiyatif alabilen, caydırıcılığı yüksek, modern ve güçlü bir vurucu güç olmasıyla da öne çıkmaktadır. Eğitimden harekata, uçuş emniyetinden idameye kadar her aşamada ortaya koyduğumuz yüksek standartlar, bu görevi en etkin şekilde icra etmemizin temel dayanağıdır."
Filonun seçkin personelinin Romanya'da görev yaparken Türkiye 'yi, Türk Silahlı Kuvvetlerini ve Türk Hava Kuvvetlerini en yüksek disiplin, itibar ve başarıyla temsil edeceğini vurgulayan Gezeravcı, "Görev süresince emniyet önceliğimizden taviz vermeden, müttefik unsurlarla tam uyum içinde çalışarak üstlendiğimiz sorumluluğu en iyi şekilde yerine getireceğiz. Bu vesileyle görev alacak tüm personelimize üstün başarılar diliyor, milletimizin gurur duyacağı, kazasız ve emniyetli bir görev dönemi temenni ediyorum." ifadesini kullandı.

Passengers advised to seek refunds via bankruptcy process, though guarantees are not assured, warns Norse Atlantic.
Norwegian budget airline Norse Atlantic said it would file for bankruptcy for its main Norwegian operating unit and has stopped selling tickets, becoming the latest airline casualty of fuel-cost spikes stemming from the war in Iran..
The airline has cancelled all flights and said on its website that its customer service department is no longer available.
The shutdown came quickly. On Wednesday, the airline, which was founded in 2021, said its financial situation was “critical”. A day later, it suspended flights and warned that it could file for bankruptcy if it failed to secure funding.
By Friday, the airline said it could not raise the money it needed to continue flying.
Norse is the latest airline to struggle with rising fuel costs brought on by the US-led war in Iran. Latvia’s airBaltic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September, while US budget airline Spirit Airlines went out of business in May.
Jet fuel prices have risen 71 percent globally over the past year and more than 78 percent in Europe, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA) which tracks jet fuel prices.
“We were unable to absorb the extra cost … Fuel is what toppled this company,” CEO Eivind Roald told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.
Norse said on its website that passengers could seek refunds through the bankruptcy process but warned that refunds were not guaranteed. It advised customers to check their travel insurance or contact their banks.
“This is a very hard day for the pilots and their families, and for all other Norse employees. Our thoughts are also with the passengers whose journeys are now cancelled,” the board of the Norse Atlantic Pilots Association told the Reuters news agency.
The airline also began ending its aircraft leasing agreements with AerCap Holdings and BOC Aviation, which were for 12 and 16 years, respectively.
Norse’s shares fell nearly 69 percent on the Oslo Stock Exchange on Friday, bringing its losses this year to 99.86 percent. In the US, its shares fell 85 percent on Friday, trading at a fraction of a cent.

Paul Mackenzie, already serving 200 years, is the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
Mackenzie was convicted on Friday in the coastal city of Mombasa, along with 29 followers, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua.
Magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie “gave the directions to fast to death”, Reuters reported. Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing.
On November 6, Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, 190 of them children. He had denied forcing the victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence.
He was also convicted this week of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and “terrorism-related offences”, according to Reuters. He is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalisation charges in December, The Associated Press reported.
Mackenzie led the Good News International Church in the Shakahola Forest, near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast.
He told followers to starve themselves and their children to death to meet Jesus before the end of the world.
Police arrested him in 2023 after a tip-off, and authorities began uncovering more than 400 bodies . People familiar with the cult told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the starvation in three phases : children first, then women and young men, and finally, the remaining men.
Mackenzie had been arrested twice before, in connection with the deaths of children, and released.
The killings have shocked Kenya and led to calls for tighter oversight of religious groups.
President William Ruto said in 2023 that he took responsibility as head of state for the government’s failure to prevent the deaths.
Other mass killings linked to cults include one in Uganda in 2000, when a doomsday group killed more than 700 people, and the 1978 massacre in Guyana, where an American cult leader ordered more than 900 followers to drink poison, Reuters said.

An official inspects the partially submerged tanker - the rescue operation is expected to be challenging
A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.
All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.
There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.
The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.
In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".
"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.
The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.
Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.
Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.
Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.
More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.
Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".
The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

The proposal comes as President Zelenskyy criticises Trump’s ‘friendship’ with Putin.
Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.
“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.
Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.
He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.
The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters , and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.
A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.
In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.
International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.
On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.
The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.
In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.
“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.
He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.
“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.
After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.
Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

Spanish women’s refusal to surrender hard-won rights helped Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez clinch an unlikely victory in a snap election three years ago. As he gambles with another early vote on Sunday, his hopes of defying the odds rest on women again rallying to block the far right from governing Spain for the first time since Francisco Franco’s dictatorship.
Kicking off his latest mission impossible at a rally in Seville, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez sported a red T-shirt with the slogan “ La fuerza de las Mujeres” (the strength of women) as he urged progressive voters to engineer an “epic comeback” at the polls.
After eight gruelling years in office, Spain ’s great political survivor knows he will need every bit of strength Spanish women can give him.
Voter surveys are predicting a decisive swing to the right in Sunday’s general election, potentially bringing a far-right party into government for the first time since Franco ’s death in 1975.
Watch more Sanchez's big gamble: Will Spain swing from Socialists to hard right?
It’s a familiar predicament for Sanchez, who has defied the odds in past elections – in large part thanks to the support of female voters determined not to surrender hard-won rights.
His Socialist Workers’ Party of Spain (PSOE) has framed the vote as a choice between “progress” and “regression”, warning that victory for a right-wing block that includes the hardline Vox party would rewind the clock to a time when Spanish women had far fewer rights.
The pitch has worked before, most recently in the last snap election Sanchez called in 2023. His chances of pulling off an even greater upset on November 29 rest largely on women's willingness to cast aside their grievances and bail him out once more.
Sanchez called the snap election on October 5 after right-wing parties voted down emergency measures his government had put together to tackle a housing crisis roiling the country.
The prime minister was hoping anger at the right for torpedoing the emergency measures would help his Socialists close the gap with the conservative Peoples’ Party (PP), which polls say is likely to secure a majority of seats in parliament in partnership with the anti-immigrant, anti-feminist Vox.
While surveys suggest the PSOE has indeed narrowed the gap, the combined left-wing bloc is still lagging far behind the joint tally of the conservatives and the far right , leaving Sanchez and his allies with a mountain to climb.

Demography is one reason the Socialists are actively courting the female vote, said Carmen Aguilera-Carnerero, a professor at the University of Granada whose research focuses on extremist rhetoric and the far right.
“There are roughly 1.2 million more women voters than there are men. That makes it a highly coveted constituency in an election that could end up being closer than expected,” she explained.
Aguilera-Carnerero said the Socialists were aiming to tap a large pool of potential voters among middle-aged women traditionally suspicious of extremist parties. She pointed to Sanchez’s widely commented appearance on the cover of a gossip magazine as part of efforts to appeal to that audience.
Sanchez has played up the legislation introduced under leftwing governments in recent decades aimed at bolstering women’s rights, such as access to abortion or better protection against gender-based violence. He has warned that a right-wing government that includes Vox would roll back decades of progress.
Watch more Violence against women: Spain's fight against domestic abuse
“Women who are in their 30s or 40s today, and have lived through different governments, are well aware of how their situation has changed and what has been achieved under left-wing governments in terms of the rights of women and minorities,” said Aguilera-Carnerero. “For many who haven’t lived through these transformations, however, the picture is perhaps less clear.”
Aguilera-Carnerero noted that “many first-time voters are unfamiliar with the Indignados Movement of 2011 – let alone the Franco era”. Young people, she added, “are looking for access to education, a job, a house, and many of them are probably not thinking so much about social rights and liberties”.
She warned that “playing the anti- fascist card” could alienate some voters and drive abstention in a country wearied by six general elections in 11 years – and also jar with the immediate concerns of many youths.
The government's failure in recent years to address the housing crisis and halt home evictions is one reason many progressive voters feel let down, said the Asambleas Feministas Abiertas de Cantabria, a feminist group based in northern Spain.
“There is fatigue, more than in 2023. People are exhausted by rent and precarity, and many feel the ‘progressive’ government didn’t deliver,” the group said in written exchanges with FRANCE 24.
“But it is fatigue with the parties, not resignation,” they added, highlighting the scale of the housing protests that have swept the country and the huge rallies against gender-based violence that took place in cities across the country this week.
Watch more Housing crisis on the ballot: Anger boils over ahead of Spanish election
“Feminist and housing movements are very active (...). The question is whether that energy turns into votes,” they added. “That depends on the left giving people a reason (to back them), not just a fear.”
While Vox's atavistic brand of macho chauvinism has long alienated female voters, surveys suggest fear of the far right has eroded in recent years, including among women.
According to polling institute 40dB, the proportion of female Vox supporters now stands at one for every 1.29 men, down from one for every 1.7 men only a year ago, narrowing the gender gap that once defined the party.
Aguilera-Carnero said Vox had recently played down some of its more divisive policies , such as repealing abortion rights or replacing the equality ministry introduced by the left with a family ministry tasked with promoting higher birth rates and traditional family values.
“That doesn’t mean their ideas have changed on these issues, but the focus has shifted,” she cautioned, noting that the party increasingly talks about the need to “protect” Spanish women.
“They claim that Spanish women need protection from outsiders, from immigrants who come from cultures that don’t respect women, and that if you stop immigration women will feel free and safe,” she explained, noting that this “femonationalist” stance was in line with other far-right movements in Europe.
Read more How far-right Vox is winning over young voters ahead of Spain's snap election
Scapegoating immigrants is one example of what Aguilera-Carnero described as the “simple solutions to complex problems” that Vox claims to offer. Such “solutions” are channelled through the party’s unmatched use of social media to reach a young and disgruntled audience, the youngest of whom have only ever known left-wing governments.
While Vox has recently made inroads among female voters, angry young men remain its largest constituency, egged on by the party’s rants against “woke” ideas, feminism and what it describes as “gender ideology”.
The rise of masculinism among young Spaniards highlights a broader educational problem that the left has so far failed to address, said the feminist Asambleas in northern Cantabria.
“We see it in schools: the manosphere, influencers, the idea that feminism ‘has gone too far’. The far right offers precarious young men someone to blame, women and migrants, instead of the real causes,” they said. “The answer needs to be education from early childhood, not punishment: sex and emotional education, coeducation, other models of masculinity.”

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez makes last bid to beat right-wing parties before Spanish vote on Sunday.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears sure he will secure a left-wing majority in ⁠a snap general election on Sunday, despite adverse public polling suggesting a right-wing advantage.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” the Socialist leader told radio station SER on Friday, as political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning before the vote.
The outcome of the election will be closely watched as Europe opens an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union.
Amid a legal ban on publishing opinion surveys within five days of an election, Sanchez ⁠insisted that internal data suggested his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.
He said that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching ‌a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.
Earlier, during a televised pre-election debate, Sanchez clashed with PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo and Vox’s Santiago Abascal, as well as Ada Colau, a left-wing Spanish politician and former mayor of Barcelona associated with the Sumar political alliance, in a debate focused on immigration, the housing crisis and foreign policy.
The prime minister criticised the Madrid regional government, controlled by the PP, for awarding an honorary medal to the Israeli government while the assault on Gaza continued.
“It is shameful,” Sanchez said, accusing his opponents of having “no humanity whatsoever.”
He also interrupted Feijoo when the conservative leader described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “massacre”, insisting that “it is genocide”.
Sanchez warned voters that Spain faced a choice between “regression and progressivism”, arguing that the PP and Vox wanted to replicate the politics of US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
Sanchez has vaunted his record on the international stage, notably his outspoken defence of immigration, clashes with Trump and criticism of Israel. The dynamism of the EU’s fourth-largest economy under his leadership has also drawn praise at a turbulent time for global markets.
Sanchez is holding his final large rally in Madrid on Friday, seeking a late mobilisation of left-wing voters to defeat what he calls the “regression” of a possible PP-Vox coalition.
“We are unstoppable and we will win!” he told a Socialist meeting in the western city of Plasencia, sporting a red T-shirt emblazoned with the slogan “the power of women”.
He contrasted a Spain “of prosperity, principles and values” against a “reactionary coalition” that would question women’s rights, cut pensions and gut public services.
PP leader Feijoo, who won the most seats at the last election in 2023 but failed to form a government, told supporters in Barcelona: “This time we will pull it off.”
Dismissing Sanchez’s campaign of “fear”, he will hold his campaign finale in Seville, capital of the southern Andalusia region.
Addressing reporters before a closing rally in the eastern city of Valencia, Vox leader Abascal accused Sanchez’s “mafia-style” government of “betraying, robbing and lying” to the country.
Spaniards will observe a “day of reflection” on the ‌eve ‌of the vote on Saturday. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.
